planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed with the onset of autumn rains across Jordan and Syria's Houran plain, the traditional rainfed method for this landrace; where autumn rains are unreliable it can also be sown in very early spring.

directions: Hourani is a tall, awned durum wheat landrace named for the Houran plain spanning southern Syria and northern Jordan, long grown as a rainfed winter cereal and preserved today in the ICARDA genebank as one of the historically important wheat landraces of the Fertile Crescent. Its hard amber kernels are prized across the region both for grinding into coarse burghul (bulgur) and, when harvested green at the soft-dough stage, for parching over fire to make freekeh, the smoky roasted-wheat staple of Levantine cuisine. Growers traditionally broadcast seed into bare, tilled ground at the start of the autumn rains and let the deep-rooted plants tiller through winter on stored soil moisture alone, since the crop is adapted to low and erratic rainfall rather than irrigation. The tall, stiff straw and modest yield compared with modern semi-dwarf durums have made Hourani increasingly rare in commercial fields, even as breeders and seed banks continue to draw on its drought tolerance and regional adaptation for arid-land wheat improvement work.
sources: ICARDA (International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas) genebank germplasm records
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations - rainfed wheat landraces of the Fertile Crescent
Jordan National Center for Agricultural Research and Extension

planting.note: Root hardwood cuttings or plant a grafted or own-rooted sapling in full sun on well-drained ground in spring; Gulosha is traditionally grown across Azerbaijan's pomegranate-growing districts alongside the related Goychay landrace group.

directions: Gulosha is a long-cultivated Azerbaijani pomegranate type, known in both pink-fruited (Gulosha Pink) and darker red-fruited (Gulosha Red) forms usually treated as sister selections of the same traditional stock. It is especially valued among Caucasus pomegranate types for its very soft, easily chewed seeds and high sugar content, qualities that made it a target for germplasm collectors cataloging Soviet-era Central Asian and Caucasian fruit genetic resources. The tree is drought-tolerant once established but produces its best fruit with a deep soak during flowering and fruit set followed by drier conditions that concentrate sugars and help prevent splitting as fruit ripens. Fruit is eaten fresh out of hand, pressed for juice, or reduced into the tart-sweet pomegranate molasses (narsharab) used throughout Azerbaijani and wider Caucasian cooking.
sources: USDA ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA - Punica granatum collection records
California Rare Fruit Growers - pomegranate variety descriptions
Azerbaijan National Academy of Sciences, Institute of Genetic Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or own-rooted vines in early spring and train onto an arbor or trellis; Dabouki is traditionally grown as a vigorous, sprawling vine in Palestinian hill-country vineyards and home gardens around Hebron.

directions: Dabouki, also transliterated Dabuki, is one of the longest-documented native grape varieties of the Palestinian hill country, long grown around Hebron, a region celebrated across the Levant for its grapes since antiquity. It produces large, loose clusters of elongated, thin-skinned green-gold berries that are eaten fresh, dried into raisins, or pressed, and the vine's vigorous, heat- and drought-tolerant habit made it a mainstay of traditional rainfed hillside vineyards long before irrigated modern table-grape cultivars arrived. Recent efforts by Palestinian agronomists and heritage-seed initiatives to catalog indigenous grape landraces have highlighted Dabouki alongside other native varieties such as Jandali and Hamdani as living agricultural heritage worth preserving. Train vines on a sturdy arbor or trellis in full sun, thin crowded clusters to improve air circulation and berry size, and expect a very vigorous, spreading vine that needs firm annual pruning to stay productive.
sources: Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture grape variety surveys
Food and Agriculture Organization - indigenous grape genetic resources of the Eastern Mediterranean
Birzeit University and Palestinian heritage-grape documentation initiatives

common_name: Vandam Walnut (Azerbaijani Thin-Shelled Heirloom Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or grafted tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Vandam is a traditional walnut selection from the Sheki-Zaqatala foothills of northwestern Azerbaijan, long propagated from seedling trees chosen for exceptionally thin shells.

directions: Vandam takes its name from a village in the walnut-rich Sheki-Zaqatala foothills of northwestern Azerbaijan, a region whose forests and dooryard orchards have supplied seedling walnut selections to the wider Caucasus for generations. It is prized above all for its remarkably thin, easily cracked shell and plump, well-filled kernel, traits that long made it a favorite dooryard and market tree even though it was traditionally propagated from seed rather than grafted onto rootstock. Like other Persian walnuts from the Caucasus it needs a cold winter dormancy and tolerates a wide range of soils but performs best in deep, well-drained loam in full sun with room for a large, round-headed canopy. Because seedling-propagated Vandam trees show more variability than cloned Western cultivars, growers who want nuts true to its famously thin-shelled type should seek out grafted stock taken from documented parent trees rather than random seedlings.
sources: Azerbaijan National Academy of Sciences, Institute of Genetic Resources - walnut germplasm records
USDA ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA - Juglans regia collection records
Food and Agriculture Organization - Caucasus walnut genetic resources reports

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree (commonly onto P. atlantica or P. terebinthus rootstock for heat and alkaline-soil tolerance) in late winter to early spring; Red Aleppo is a traditional Syrian pistachio selection from the historic Aleppo growing region and needs a male pollenizer planted nearby since pistachios are dioecious.

directions: Red Aleppo is a traditional pistachio selection from the historic orchards around Aleppo, Syria, one of the oldest pistachio-growing regions in the world and long a source of planting material for pistachio culture across the wider Mediterranean. It became internationally significant as the open-pollinated seed parent of Sirora, the even-bearing cultivar Australia's CSIRO released from Red Aleppo stock that now accounts for roughly half of Australia's pistachio acreage. Like other pistachios it is dioecious, so a male tree must be planted nearby for pollination, and it needs hot, dry summers together with roughly 1,000 hours of winter chill below about 45 degrees Fahrenheit to properly fill and split its shells. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, and expect several years of establishment before the tree begins bearing a meaningful crop.
sources: CSIRO - Sirora pistachio cultivar release documentation
Australian Pistachio Growers' Association variety information
Food and Agriculture Organization - pistachio genetic resources of the Eastern Mediterranean
